config.title: Networking fundamentals

intro.title: Networking fundamentals
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple network diagram to visualize how data travels between devices. You'll learn the core concept of network layers, which organize communication into distinct levels like physical connections and logical addressing. The main technologies involved include IP addresses, routers, and packet switching. By the end, you'll understand how networks are structured and how information moves reliably across the internet.
intro.usecase: Networking fundamentals are the backbone of every modern web application, enabling features like real-time chat in messaging apps, live data updates in financial dashboards, and seamless media streaming in video platforms. As a production engineer, you'll apply these concepts to design resilient systems that handle millions of concurrent connections, optimize data transfer for global e-commerce sites, and troubleshoot latency in user-facing services like online gaming or video conferencing. Mastering these principles ensures you can build scalable, reliable infrastructure that powers everything from social media feeds to cloud-based collaboration tools.

objectives: Implement a basic network request handler to process incoming data
Configure network connection parameters for different communication protocols
Construct a simple client-server model to demonstrate data exchange
Initialize network sockets for bidirectional communication
Apply error handling mechanisms for network connectivity issues
Manipulate network packet structures to optimize data transmission
Integrate network monitoring tools to track connection status

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package to set up your component with state management capabilities.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and hooks
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component file will have the necessary imports to use React and manage state with useState.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to import both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: import React and useState from the 'react' package to proceed.

steps.title: Create the main NetworkingFundamentals component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named NetworkingFundamentals that returns null initially.
steps.hint: Define a component that can later contain networking-related UI. Start with a simple return statement.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';
// Create the NetworkingFundamentals component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A component named NetworkingFundamentals is defined and returns null.
successCriteria: The NetworkingFundamentals component is created as a function that returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a component named NetworkingFundamentals that returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Create a function named NetworkingFundamentals that returns null.

steps.title: Initialize state for network protocol selection
steps.instruction: Inside your NetworkingFundamentals component, use useState to create a state variable called 'selectedProtocol' initialized to 'TCP'.
steps.hint: Call useState with the initial value 'TCP' and destructure the returned array into the state variable and setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing state for a selected option
const [selectedOption, setSelectedOption] = useState('default');
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'selectedProtocol' that tracks which network protocol is currently selected, starting with 'TCP'.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with 'TCP' as the initial value, and the returned array is destructured into 'selectedProtocol' and 'setSelectedProtocol'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with 'TCP' as the initial value and destructuring the array correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The state initialization is missing or incorrect. Use useState('TCP') and destructure the array into [selectedProtocol, setSelectedProtocol].

steps.title: Define protocol data structure
steps.instruction: Inside your component, create a constant array named 'protocols' containing objects for TCP, UDP, and HTTP with name, description, and port properties.
steps.hint: Define the array before the return statement. Each object should have three properties: name (string), description (string), and port (number).
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a protocols array with three protocol objects, each containing name, description, and port properties.
successCriteria: The protocols array is defined with three objects containing name, description, and port properties for TCP, UDP, and HTTP.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your array has exactly three objects with name, description, and port properties for TCP, UDP, and HTTP.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a constant array named 'protocols' with three objects representing TCP, UDP, and HTTP protocols, each with name, description, and port properties.

steps.title: Create protocol selection handler
steps.instruction: Define a function named handleProtocolSelect that takes a protocol parameter and updates the selectedProtocol state with it.
steps.hint: Inside your component, create a function that uses the setSelectedProtocol function from useState to update the state.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleProtocolSelect function that updates the selectedProtocol state when called with a protocol parameter.
successCriteria: The handleProtocolSelect function is defined and calls setSelectedProtocol with its parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your function takes a protocol parameter and calls setSelectedProtocol with it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't defined correctly. It should take a protocol parameter and update the state using setSelectedProtocol.

steps.title: Add main container structure
steps.instruction: Return a div with className 'networking-container' from your NetworkingFundamentals component.
steps.hint: Replace the current return value (null) with a div element that has the specified className.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a div element with className 'networking-container' as the main layout container.
successCriteria: The component returns a div element with className 'networking-container'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning a div element with exactly className='networking-container'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should return a div element with className 'networking-container'. Check your syntax and make sure you're replacing the current return value.

steps.title: Create protocol selection buttons
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, map through the protocols array to create a button for each protocol. Each button should display the protocol name and call handleProtocolSelect when clicked.
steps.hint: Use the map method on the protocols array to generate buttons. Each button needs an onClick handler that calls handleProtocolSelect with the protocol name.
steps.expectedOutcome: Three interactive buttons labeled 'TCP', 'UDP', and 'HTTP' will appear in the UI, each wired to update the selectedProtocol state when clicked.
successCriteria: The protocols array is mapped to create buttons with proper onClick handlers that call handleProtocolSelect with the protocol name.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're mapping through the protocols array and each button has an onClick handler that calls handleProtocolSelect with the protocol name.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons aren't properly implemented. Remember to use the map method on the protocols array and wire each button's onClick to handleProtocolSelect.

steps.title: Display selected protocol details
steps.instruction: Add a section after the introduction paragraph that displays the name, description, and default port of the selectedProtocol when a protocol is selected.
steps.hint: You can use conditional rendering to check if selectedProtocol has a value, then find the matching protocol object from the protocols array to display its details.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show protocol details (name, description, and port) when a protocol is selected, and nothing when no protocol is selected.
successCriteria: A conditional display section is added that shows the selected protocol's name, description, and default port when selectedProtocol has a value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some display logic, but make sure to include all three details (name, description, and port) and handle the case when no protocol is selected.
steps.feedbackWrong: The protocol details display isn't working correctly. Check that you're using conditional rendering and accessing the correct properties from the protocols array.

steps.title: Add visual indicator for selected protocol
steps.instruction: Add conditional styling to the protocol selection buttons to highlight the currently selected protocol. Use inline styling with a background color to visually distinguish the active button.
steps.hint: In the button's style attribute, check if the protocol name matches selectedProtocol. If it does, apply a background color like 'lightblue'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Conditional styling example
<button style={{ backgroundColor: isActive ? 'lightblue' : 'white' }}>
  Click me
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The selected protocol button will have a distinct background color, providing clear visual feedback to the user.
successCriteria: Each protocol button has conditional styling that applies a background color when its protocol matches selectedProtocol.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some styling, but make sure the background color only applies when the protocol matches selectedProtocol.
steps.feedbackWrong: The selected protocol button doesn't have conditional styling. Add inline styling that checks if protocol.name equals selectedProtocol.
